clue.text: Matches finally drawn ? These always are

definitions.text: Matches finally drawn ? These always are

parts.words: Matches finally drawn ? These always are
parts.note: at the close of every cricket match the wooden uprights of the wicket are pulled up, so these items are always drawn at the end

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark that every contest ends in a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' suggests a tied result, but at close of play in cricket the umpires pull up the wicket's uprights: 'drawing' them ends every match, won or drawn.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the uprights of the wicket are pulled from the ground at close of play, which happens to every match.

clue.text: Hammer-thrower a girl.

parts.note: the Norse thunder god threw his hammer Mjölnir

explanation.surface: An athlete in the hammer event is a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The hammer-thrower is not an athlete but the Norse god, whose hammer returned after each throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Mother Superior ?

parts.note: read not as the head of a convent but as a mother who rules a family

explanation.surface: The head of a convent.
explanation.walkthrough: A Mother Superior heads a convent; here the phrase means a mother who is in charge of her family.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who heads a family or clan is literally a ruling mother.

clue.text: Miss Australia

parts.note: read not as a beauty title but as the everyday Australian slang word for any young woman

explanation.surface: The winner of a national beauty contest.
explanation.walkthrough: A beauty-queen title is suggested, but this is the Australian slang word for a girl or woman: any miss in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang for a young woman, so an Aussie miss.

clue.text: Miser's failing to put up one penny once, in the City

indicators.note: the clue tells us to put the other pieces in the city, so they go inside its letters

parts.note: the City is the financial district of London, here spelt out as written
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I
d was the abbreviation for the old pre-decimal penny

explanation.surface: A miser refuses to contribute even a penny in the financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: D, from the Latin denarius, stood for a penny before British decimalisation in 1971, hence 'once'. 'To put' and 'the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed for money is exactly the weakness a miser shows; the word names avarice.

clue.text: Scene of many board meetings

parts.note: not company directors at a table, but players meeting over the chequered board in a competition

explanation.surface: A corporate headquarters where directors gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board meetings' suggests company directors; the board is a chessboard, and many games are played at a competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitive event where many games are played over the chequered board.

clue.text: Not little fishcakes

parts.note: the word looks as if it means small specimens of a freshwater fish, but it names a griddle cake instead

explanation.surface: A diner complaining the fishcakes are too big.
explanation.walkthrough: The word looks like 'little pikes', but it is a small thick pancake or crumpet, so these are cakes without fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Small griddle pancakes, so cakes that are not little fish despite the name.

clue.text: Use a fork on it — or a finger

definitions.meaning: an instruction to work the ground with a garden fork, read as two words
a finger or toe, each counted as one unit of the hand or foot

explanation.surface: Table manners: eat it with a fork or your fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: The fork is a garden fork, not cutlery: split the answer as DIG IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A finger is one of the hand's digits; split in two, the word is also an order to turn over the soil.

clue.text: End of long journey for generous diner on a railway

parts.note: a diner who leaves a generous gratuity is a tipper

explanation.surface: A big-tipping diner reaches the end of a long railway trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the First World War song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary'. 'On' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish town is the destination of the famous marching song about a long way to go.

clue.text: Not what to expect in Cork on the contrary

definitions.text: Not what to expect in Cork on the contrary

parts.words: Not what to expect in Cork on the contrary
parts.note: a cork is what you expect to find in the narrow neck of a wine vessel, not the other way about

explanation.surface: A traveller's warning about something unusual in the Irish city of Cork.
explanation.walkthrough: Cork reads as the Irish city; it is a stopper, which sits in the narrow neck of a bottle rather than the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrow top part of a wine container is where a cork goes, so it contains the cork rather than being in it.

clue.text: Some doctors need a filling for vacancies

indicators.note: the letter is to be a filling, so it goes inside the doctors' letters

parts.note: GPs are general practitioners, family doctors

explanation.surface: Doctors needing a dental filling to fill gaps in their staff.
explanation.walkthrough: GP, for general practitioner, is the British term for a family doctor. 'Need' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacancies are empty spaces or openings, the same as holes or breaks.

clue.text: A cub's ill-possible cause

indicators.note: a possible arrangement of the letters signals that they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering what might have made a young animal sick.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of A CUBS ILL, signalled by 'possible', gives the germ, and the whole clue describes it: a possible cause of a cub's illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A rod-shaped bacterium can be the source of infection that makes an animal sick.

clue.text: Untidy little beasts

definitions.meaning: to mess up a place with scattered rubbish
a brood of young animals born together

explanation.surface: A complaint about messy young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: To strew rubbish is to make untidy, and a mother animal's brood of young shares the same word.

clue.text: Tailed Scottish gentleman to a retreat

indicators.note: having had the tail docked, the gentleman's last letter is removed

parts.note: a laird is a Scottish landowner

explanation.surface: A Scottish gent in a tailcoat heading off to his hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailed' looks like 'wearing tails' but means 'with the tail cut off', as with tailing beans. 'To a' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A den or hideout is a place one withdraws to, a retreat.

clue.text: Awful peril for banner-bearing youth

parts.note: in Longfellow's poem Excelsior the youth carrying a banner is warned to beware the awful snowslide

explanation.surface: A danger facing a young flag-carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: In Longfellow's poem 'Excelsior', a youth carries a banner up the Alps and is warned: 'Beware the awful avalanche!'
explanation.definitionFit: A mass of snow sliding down a mountain is the peril the poem's climbing youth is warned against.

clue.text: "Dress ——" seldom means this (except on Brighton beach ?)

definitions.text: "Dress ——" seldom means this (except on Brighton beach ?)

parts.words: "Dress ——" seldom means this (except on Brighton beach ?)
parts.note: on an invitation, a note saying formal wear is not required rarely means wearing nothing at all, except at a naturist beach

explanation.surface: A joke about party invitations and a seaside nudist beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank in the printed clue is the answer itself. Brighton, a resort on England's south coast, has a well-known naturist beach where clothes really are not required.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left to choice is not compulsory, which on an invitation means guests may decide how to dress.

clue.text: Not even Don is a member of society

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd
a fellow is a senior member of a college, as is a don

explanation.surface: Not even a university lecturer belongs to society.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oddfellows are a friendly society, a British mutual-aid association, so a member is one of them. 'Is a' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oddfellows are a long-established friendly society, a mutual benefit club whose members bear its name.

clue.text: Stage wife shows how to win at 5 dn

definitions.meaning: a partner in a theatrical production, an actor's companion on stage

definitions.text: shows how to win at 5 dn
definitions.meaning: the clue refers to the chess entry at 5 down: deliver checkmate to win

explanation.surface: An actress playing a wife shows how to win a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as PLAY MATE: 'play' is stage and 'mate' is wife, and at chess (5 down) you win by playing mate.
explanation.definitionFit: A companion in play; as two words, play and mate mean act and spouse, and also the winning move in chess.

clue.text: Button-hole for one of his buttons?

definitions.text: Button-hole for one of his buttons?

parts.words: Button-hole for one of his buttons?
parts.note: a flower called by an unmarried man's name, his buttons, is worn in the lapel as a buttonhole

explanation.surface: A question about stitching holes for a man's coat buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: A buttonhole is also a flower worn in a lapel; 'bachelor's buttons' is a cottage-garden flower, so it could be one.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried man gives his name to the flower known as his buttons.

clue.text: Times of bewilderment, it's said

indicators.note: this says the word for bewilderment is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a daze is a state of bewilderment

explanation.surface: Recalling confusing periods of one's life.
explanation.definitionFit: Times in the sense of eras or periods, as in 'in olden times'.

clue.text: Seven sisters at the seaside, all in white

definitions.text: Seven sisters at the seaside, all in white

parts.words: Seven sisters at the seaside, all in white
parts.note: not seven siblings in white dresses but a run of chalk headlands on the Sussex coast

explanation.surface: Seven sisters dressed in white on a beach outing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Seven Sisters are a line of white chalk headlands on England's Sussex coast, near Beachy Head.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep rock faces by the sea; the Seven Sisters are white chalk ones.

clue.text: Annual call for help

definitions.meaning: the first of May, a spring festival held every year

explanation.surface: A distress call that comes round once a year.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring festival on the first of May recurs every year, and the same phrase is the radio distress signal.

clue.text: It's an awful feeling

parts.note: read literally, a feeling full of awe or fear rather than simply an unpleasant one

explanation.surface: A complaint about feeling bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' means bad in everyday use, but here it means full of awe: fear and apprehension.
explanation.definitionFit: Great fear or apprehension is a feeling filled with awe in the old sense.

clue.text: People are well rid of them

definitions.text: People are well rid of them

parts.words: People are well rid of them
parts.note: read literally, people who are well have got rid of these, rather than being glad to be free of something

explanation.surface: A remark about unwanted things one is glad to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well rid of' sounds like the idiom for being glad to lose something, but it means that being well is being rid of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Illnesses are what a healthy person no longer has.

clue.text: List of furniture in The Nest?

definitions.meaning: a set of data in rows and columns, as in a league standings chart
a nest is a set of small stacking pieces of furniture that fit one under another

explanation.surface: An inventory of the furniture in a house called The Nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Nest' looks like a house name, but a nest of tables is a set that slides one under another.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart of figures in rows is one sense; the stacking items in a nest are pieces of furniture of the same name.

clue.text: Top came adrift

indicators.note: letters that have come adrift are loose and out of place, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lid or garment came loose.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or peak of something is its summit.

clue.text: High honour for St James's top establishment

definitions.meaning: in card games the honours are the top cards, and the highest in a suit is the ace
St James's is the London district of gentlemen's clubs, so the best of those clubs

explanation.surface: Praise for the finest gentleman's club in a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: St James's in London is famous for its gentlemen's clubs, so the top one there is the best of clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest card in one suit is a top honour in bridge, and the phrase also suits the leading gentlemen's club.

clue.text: Exhausted — conducting the "Marche Funèbre"?

definitions.meaning: a conductor beating time for a funeral march beats for those who have died

explanation.surface: A conductor worn out after leading a funeral march.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Marche Funèbre' is the funeral march, as in Chopin's piano sonata; conducting it means beating time for the departed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worn out completely is a colloquial meaning; the second reading is time beaten for those who have died.

clue.text: He gets his teeth into his job

definitions.text: He gets his teeth into his job

parts.words: He gets his teeth into his job
parts.note: the teeth belong to the worker's tool, a blade with a toothed edge that bites into timber

explanation.surface: Praise for an eager, committed worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets his teeth into' sounds like enthusiasm, but the teeth are those of a saw cutting wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who cuts timber with a toothed blade does exactly this as his trade.
